business: Eat Out Better, an iPhone app that rates every dish on a restaurant menu for high cholesterol
by_segment: Newly diagnosed, motivated (told in the last year)
Caregiver or spouse ordering for a partner
why_not: I already know what to order after twenty years on a statin, and I'm not going to hold my phone up over a menu in front of my wife or clients. The free scan is nice, but I'd delete it after the first use because I'd never use it at the table.
My statin handles my cholesterol and I already know to order the grilled fish or the salad. I don't need a phone app to tell me what I already do on autopilot.

I already photograph menus and ask an AI assistant what's in a dish, and that's free. I don't see why I'd pay for a narrower app that promises to rate every dish, when I'd have to trust its guess about how a restaurant cooks.

I'd run the free scan out of curiosity, but I won't pay a yearly fee for ratings from an app with no doctor or dietitian behind them. I also cancel anything that auto-renews after a trial, so this would be a no from me.

My statin already handles my cholesterol, and I don't stress about restaurants. I'd try the free first scan out of curiosity, but I wouldn't pay $39.99 a year for something I can mostly get by asking ChatGPT with a photo of the menu.

My first thought is that I can just ask ChatGPT for free. I already snap pictures of things and ask an assistant what's in them, so a separate iPhone app that does one narrow job feels like paying for something I can get elsewhere.
I eat out with my wife on weekends and I'm not going to pull out my phone and photograph a menu at the table while we're trying to talk. It feels like a chore, and it would look odd to our friends.

I eat out with friends and clients, and I am not going to pull out my phone to photograph a menu in front of them. I've managed my cholesterol for years by ordering the grilled fish and asking for sauce on the side, and I can do that without an app.
I'm not going to hold my phone up at a table and scan a menu in front of my friends and the staff. I like the numbers, but this app gives me colours and not grams, so I'd still be guessing.

I already log everything in MyFitnessPal and I like numbers. A green, yellow or red dot with 'fried, cream sauce' is a vague label, and the app says up front it does not count grams, so it would not tell me what I actually want to know.
flip: If my doctor told me my numbers were still high despite the statin and I needed to change how I eat out, and the app's ratings matched what my doctor and dietitian would say.
If I could scan the menu at home from the restaurant's website or a PDF, without anyone seeing me do it, and it showed actual calories and saturated fat per dish.
Proof that its ratings match real restaurant recipes or lab-tested nutrition data, for example a published accuracy check against dishes that were actually measured.
If I could scan the menu at home before going out and show the top picks on my phone at the table, without taking a photo in the restaurant.
If it showed me that the grilled fish I always order is actually cooked in butter or cream, something I had no idea about, and I could fix it with one swap.
If I could get the answer without taking out my phone at the table, and it were clearly better than what I get from asking ChatGPT for free.
A named clinician or registered dietitian standing behind the ratings, plus a plan that does not auto-renew after the trial.
My dietitian or doctor recommends it, or the free scans turn out to match what she tells me about specific dishes.
If it showed me that a grilled dish I order every time, like the salmon, actually comes with something on it that I didn't expect, I'd pay for that.
If it showed estimated cholesterol-relevant numbers per dish, like saturated fat or LDL-related grams, that I could log next to my tracker.
A clear statement that the advice is reviewed by a doctor or registered dietitian, plus a way to use it without taking my phone out at the table.
Proof that it's clearly more accurate than a general AI assistant on real restaurant menus, for example a side-by-side test showing it catches cream sauces and frying that ChatGPT misses.
A named dietitian or doctor behind the ratings, plus a clear note on how the green, yellow and red calls are made. I'd also try the free first scan before paying anything.
A one-time price with no renewal, or proof over a few free scans that it catches the dishes I actually order and isn't just flagging everything red.
If I could check the menu on my phone at home before I go out, without having to scan anything at the table.
A way to check the menu at home before I go out, with no photo in public and no subscription to remember to cancel.
A named doctor or registered dietitian behind the ratings, plus proof the ratings match what the dishes actually contain.
My dietitian or cardiologist recommending it, plus proof that the ratings match what the kitchen actually cooks.
If it showed me something ChatGPT can't, like a verified list of cholesterol numbers for each dish from the restaurant itself, I'd try it for a month.
My cardiologist or dietitian recommending it to me, or the free top-3 picks proving accurate enough that I don't feel I need to pay to see the rest of the menu.
